appropriate

/uh-PROH-pree-ayt/ - the stress falls on PROH · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Appropriate means to take something for one's own use, often without permission.

The stationmaster quietly appropriated coal from the railway's winter store to heat his own cottage, a scuttle or two at a time.

Example

When the botanical society disbanded, its secretary appropriated the rare orchid collection for his own greenhouse, recording the plants in the final minutes as 'lost to frost.'

Appropriate the verb (uh-PROH-pree-AYT) is not the adjective meaning 'suitable.' As a verb it means to take for yourself, often quietly and often under cover of a title or a form — which makes it sound tamer than 'steal' while meaning much the same thing.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

commandeer: Commandeer is seizure done openly, with official muscle behind it — troops commandeer a barn, police commandeer a passing cab. Appropriate is quieter: it takes for one's own use under cover of a title, a ledger, or a form, and hopes nobody thinks to ask.

pilfer: To pilfer is to make small, sneaky, repeated thefts — a stamp here, a button there — with no paperwork and no excuse offered. Appropriate is the white-collar cousin: whoever appropriates takes under some claim of office or right, so the taking looks almost proper on paper.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

return: to give back what was taken

restore: to put it back where it belonged, made whole

Where it sits · how wrongfully the taking is done — borrow → appropriate → plunder

borrow vs. appropriate: To borrow is open and temporary — permission asked, the thing returned; borrow stops far short of appropriate, which takes for keeps and asks nobody.

plunder vs. appropriate: Plunder goes further than appropriate: an official appropriates supplies with a signature and a straight face, while an army plunders a town openly and by force.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ap-

Prefix — ap-: to, toward

Root — propri

Root — propri: one's own

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: to make, to do

Put it together

Put it together: Ap- (to) + propri- (one's own) + -ate (to make) = to make something your own. Latin proprius, 'one's own,' also gives English property and proper; appropriate the verb is that root in motion — moving what belongs to someone else into the column marked mine.

Use the root in a new word: property

Word Choice

formal / bureaucratic

Appropriate flourishes wherever ledgers and titles do — officials appropriate funds, supplies, and credit. Beside it, usurp (also in this unit) takes offices and powers rather than goods. And mind the stress: to appropri-ATE (verb) is shady; APP-ropriate (adjective, 'suitable') is blameless.
